title: Bourbon and Bullet Holes
synopsis: 0247 on a Wednesday. Pixel hears Kyle's footfall on the stairs, thinks bourbon, opens her door, and finds him bleeding through his coat in a way that is not bourbon at all. She brings him into Unit 2E, gets him onto Maeve, and works for ninety minutes — first the bullet, then the cyberware she discovers underneath: a misfiring NeoCortex lateral array node that has been quietly making him hate his own thoughts for six days. She fixes it with a piece of solder and a drop of conductive paste. He says her name right.
html:
# Bourbon and Bullet Holes

It was 0247.

It was Wednesday, which Pixel knew because she had been three weeks past the previous Wednesday — three weeks past the noodle bag, three weeks past the angle in the stairwell, three weeks past *Kyle, six foot, seven sentences*. They had spoken at the angle four more times since. None of the conversations had gone past nine sentences. None of them had gone backwards either.

She was at Maeve, which is to say she was *home*, and the wall was singing softly because she had the music at three-quarter volume and the radiator at the same level it always ran, and she was reflowing a connector on a 4-line bus board that belonged to a man on the third floor who needed it back by morning. Her shit-kicker boots were off, on the mat by the door. Her enormous sweater — the *real* one, the heathered grey, the one she had decided two months ago was the only sweater that mattered — was over her hands. The right wrist gyrostabilizer was three months old, still healing, and made a tiny *purr* under fine work that nobody else could hear.

She heard the footfall on the stairs.

It was 2F's footfall — the eleven-beat one — but it was *wrong*. Off-tempo. The third step had been doubled. The fifth step had skipped. The seventh step had landed too hard. Pixel's hands stopped moving on the bus board and her head turned a quarter-inch toward the door without her telling it to.

*Drunk,* she thought, and then she thought, *no,* and the *no* arrived with a small clean panic she had not asked for.

She set the iron down.

She was at the door before she had fully decided to be at the door. She opened it.

Kyle was at the top of the stairs. He had stopped. He was using the wall. The wall was holding him up by exactly the surface of his right shoulder and a smear of his right palm.

The wall, Pixel registered, was darker than wall.

*Not bourbon.*

"Hi," she said. Light. Not a question. Light because alarm in this moment would have been an *insult* — this man did not need her surprise; he needed her hands.

"Sorry," Kyle said. His voice had the careful carved precision of a person who had practiced his words on the way up the stairs. "Wrong floor."

"This is your floor."

"Right."

"Come here."

He didn't move.

She walked the four steps to him. She did not touch him. She got under his right arm — the one that was not currently a wall-prop — and let him decide whether to lean. He leaned. She felt his weight settle, and the weight told her three things in one second: *upper torso, left side, wet.*

"Two-E," she said. "Maeve has good light. Come on."

"I'll bleed on it."

"Maeve's bled on before. Maeve forgives."

She got him into the unit. She got him onto Maeve, which was the right surface — the workbench had a clean steel laminate that she could wipe in one stroke, and a lip around the edge that caught fluids before fluids became a problem on the floor, and Pixel had not, when she'd named the workbench Maeve, anticipated this exact use case, but Maeve, like all good tools, was what you needed her to be when you needed her.

She killed the music with one hand.

She did not narrate yet. She would narrate; she always narrated when working. But the first sixty seconds of any field assessment was for the body, not for the mouth. She got the coat off — *one round, left lat, low,* she logged silently; *exit, yes, exit, also low, also clean* — and the shirt up. The bleed had slowed because of the cold and the angle and the meat that had stopped most of the round on the way through. She would have called it lucky if she had been the kind of medic who used that word. She was not.

"Hold still," she said, finally, out loud, when she had the surgical light on and the field of work clean. "I said hold still. I know you don't need me to say it. The narrating is for me."

"Okay."

"Tell me what hit you."

"Jacketed nine. Civilian."

"Through?"

"Through. Vest caught most of it. The lat got the rest."

"Not a vital. Decent angle. You got *lucky*, Kyle. Don't argue with me."

"I wasn't going to."

She worked.

She pulled the round's path open with two clamps and a finger and got the fragment that had stopped half-in — *jacketed, deformed, but whole, no sloughing* — and dropped it onto the steel of Maeve, and Maeve made a small flat *plink*, which was the right sound, the *good news* sound. She irrigated. She closed. She used the ChromaSeal because she had three left and this was a chromaseal injury, and Kyle did not flinch at the sting, which most people did, which told her something about Kyle she had already half-known and now formally filed.

The bullet hole was forty-five minutes.

The other thing took longer.

She found it because she was running her diagnostic clip — *Auntie's clip,* she still thought of it as Auntie's clip, three years later, the foil packet long since returned to the canvas roll with a small handwritten label inside — over the base of his skull as a precaution. She did this with everyone post-trauma. She was not looking for anything in particular. She had decided, at fifteen, that you ran the clip every time, because the time you didn't run it was the time you missed something.

The clip beeped. Then it beeped *wrong*.

*Wrong* in the diagnostic sense; not loud, not alarming, just — a tone she had not expected, in a frequency that meant *recheck this.*

She rechecked. She rechecked again.

The lateral array — the cluster of contact pads that sat behind his right ear, that handled the cross-talk between his NeoCortex implant and his autonomic baseline, that was responsible for *the boundary between his own signal and the bleed of everything else* — had three nodes glowing in thermal stress.

Not acute. Not red. Yellow, the steady patient yellow of *this has been failing for days and you have been ignoring it.*

"Kyle," she said. Quiet. Even. She did not stop scanning.

"Yeah."

"Your lateral array is running hot."

A silence.

She waited it out.

"How long," she said, "have you known about this."

The silence got longer. She watched the back of his neck, which was the only part of his face she could see right now. She watched the small muscle at the base of his jaw go *still*, which was not the same as relaxed.

"Six days."

"Six days."

"Maybe seven."

"Were you going to tell me."

"It's calibrating itself."

"Kyle. *No.* It is *not.*" She set the clip down, because the clip was not the conversation now; the conversation was. She came around to the side of the bench so he could see her face, because she had decided that this part required eye contact. "Lateral arrays do not calibrate themselves out of a thermal stress profile. They calibrate themselves *into* one. If your delta-sync drops past eight percent variance — and it is at six right now, Kyle, you are *two points* from the edge — you start to lose the boundary between your own signal and the bleed. You start to confuse what is yours and what is *not yours.* The thing you don't like in your own head gets louder. The voice that says — the voice that —" She stopped. "You know what voice I mean."

He looked at her.

For exactly two seconds, the cataloging went away. There was something else underneath the cataloging, and then the cataloging came back.

"I know," he said.

"Six days, Kyle."

"I know."

"I am going to fix it. Right now. Lie back down."

He lay back down.

She ran a parallel jumper to bypass the failing nodes. She isolated the worst of the three. She pulled the contact pad — bone-handled probe, brass-fitted, *her mother's* probe, the one with the slight burr on the rim that her mother had worn smooth with her thumb over twenty years — and lifted the pad out and saw, immediately, the problem: a microfracture across the conductive trace, the kind you got from the unit running hot for six days and then cooling down too fast and then running hot again. The *sloppy* fracture. The fracture you got from a person not respecting their own equipment.

She fixed it with a piece of solder the size of a grain of rice and a drop of conductive paste from a tube she kept on Maeve in a little stand she had named *Reliquary*. She seated the pad back. She closed the array. She let the clip recheck.

The tone was *right.*

She sat back. She put the brass-handled probe down. She let her hands stop.

"Done," she said.

"What was it."

"Microfracture in the third lateral. Six days of you ignoring it. A drop of paste. Two minutes."

"It's been —"

"Loud. I know."

A beat.

A second beat, longer than the first.

"Pixel," Kyle said. *Pixel.* Not *Vera.* Not *Hey.* Not *the girl across the hall.* It was the first time he had said her name with the specific flatness he reserved for things he had decided to commit to memory.

"Yeah."

"Thanks."

It was the first time he had said *thanks.*

She heard it. She filed it. She did not, by the smallest available muscle, react.

"It's six hundred Quanta if I bill you," she said, instead. "It's two cucumbers and a sentence I can use in a fight if I don't."

"Cucumbers," he said.

"It's a system."

"Two cucumbers."

"That's the going rate. Don't argue with me about your own bill."

He was quiet a long time. He was looking at the ceiling. The ceiling was not interesting; it was the ceiling of Unit 2E, which had a hairline crack in the plaster that had been there since 2147 and would be there in 2300.

"I'll bring two cucumbers," he said.

"Tomorrow's fine."

He sat up slowly. The bullet hole hurt; she watched the muscle at his jaw register the exact frequency of pain and decide not to spend it. He pulled his shirt back together, and it was a wreck, and he handled it with the small dignity of a person who had decided the shirt could be a wreck and his manner could not.

At the door, with the night outside it, he paused.

"Pixel," he said.

"Yeah."

"Don't tell anyone you fixed the array."

"I haven't told anyone anything since 2217."

He nodded. Once.

He crossed the hall to 2F. He went in. The door closed.

She stood for a minute with her hand on her own doorframe.

She went back inside. She washed Maeve. She put the brass-handled probe back in the canvas roll. She added a small clean note to the brick wall, in the marker, under all the other notes:

*2F. Lateral array, third node. Fixed. He said it right.*

She stood back from the wall. She did not, at first, feel anything in particular. The feeling came later, the way it always did with her — slow, on a delay, arriving when she was about to fall asleep — and when it came it was not the feeling she had expected.

She had expected joy. She had expected the small bright satisfaction of a thing fixed.

What she got was the quiet sad warm thing that you got when you understood, all at once, that a person you had been politely curious about had been *quietly hurting* across the hall from you for six days and had not asked, and that he was the kind of person who would never ask, and that the asking — the *not* asking — was a wound of its own, and you were now *responsible* for it, in a small private way that did not require his permission.

She lay on the floor next to Maeve. The radiator ran softly. The wall, she could see in the half-light, was filling up.

*Oh,* she thought.

*Oh, this is what this is.*

She did not name it. Naming it would have been overstepping. She let it be the unnamed thing it was.

In the morning, on her doormat, there were two cucumbers in a paper bag and a folded slip of paper. The paper said, in narrow careful handwriting she would later learn was Kyle's:

*The going rate. Plus a sentence: I owe you, and the building knows it.*

She added the slip to the canvas roll.

She added one more line to the wall, a small one, near the bottom, where she would see it every morning:

*The door is unlocked.*

She meant her own.

She meant it on purpose.
